title: String Matching Algorithms
tagline: Finding a pattern inside a text efficiently — from search engines to DNA sequencing, string matching is one of computing's most practical problems.

sections.content:
String matching asks: given a text T of length n and a pattern P of length m, find all positions in T where P occurs. The brute-force approach tries every starting position — O(n·m) worst case — acceptable for small inputs but catastrophically slow for large texts or adversarial inputs.

Three algorithms span the complexity landscape. The **naive algorithm** is O(n·m) but needs no preprocessing. **Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP)** preprocesses the pattern to build a **failure function** in O(m), then searches in O(n) — total O(n+m). **Rabin-Karp** uses a **rolling hash** to check windows of text in O(1) amortised — total O(n+m) expected, O(n·m) worst case (rare with a good hash). Understanding these algorithms builds intuition for preprocessing, amortised analysis, and hash functions that appear throughout computer science.

sections.title: Looking for a Word in a Book
sections.content:
Imagine searching a book for the word 'ABCABD'. The naive approach reads character by character from every page position, comparing character by character. If a mismatch occurs, you slide one position and start over — you throw away all the comparison work you just did.

KMP is smarter: it studies the pattern *before searching*. It notices 'ABC' appears at the start of the pattern and again at position 3 ('ABCABD'). When a mismatch occurs after matching 'ABCAB', instead of restarting from scratch, KMP knows the 'AB' at the end of what it already matched is the same as the 'AB' at the start of the pattern — so it can slide to position 2 rather than position 0 and keep going.

Rabin-Karp takes a completely different approach: it converts each window of text into a hash (a number fingerprint) and compares hashes. Instead of comparing characters, it checks fingerprints — far cheaper for large patterns.

**Naive algorithm**: for each starting position i from 0 to n-m, compare T[i..i+m-1] with P[0..m-1]. If all m characters match, record a hit; otherwise try position i+1. Worst case: text is 'AAAA…A' and pattern is 'AAA…AB' — every position matches m-1 characters before failing, giving O(n·m).

**KMP algorithm** eliminates redundant comparisons by precomputing the **failure function** (also called the partial match table) `lps[j]`: the length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..j] that is also a suffix. When a mismatch occurs at pattern position j, instead of resetting j to 0, reset to `lps[j-1]` — reusing the overlap knowledge. Building lps takes O(m) using a two-pointer technique. Searching takes O(n) because the text pointer `i` never moves backwards. Total: O(n+m), guaranteed worst case.

**Rabin-Karp** computes a hash of the first window T[0..m-1] and of P. It slides the window right using a **rolling hash**: remove the leftmost character's contribution and add the new rightmost character in O(1). If hashes match, do a full character comparison to confirm (avoiding hash collisions). The rolling hash uses polynomial rolling: `hash = (s[0]*b^(m-1) + s[1]*b^(m-2) + ... + s[m-1]) mod q`. Removing s[0] and adding s[m]: `new_hash = (old_hash - s[0]*b^(m-1)) * b + s[m]`. Expected O(n+m); worst case O(n·m) if many hash collisions (extremely rare in practice with a large prime q).

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: buildLPS fills lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix. For 'ABABCABAB': lps[1]=0 (only 'AB', no match), lps[2]=1 ('ABA' — 'A' is prefix=suffix), lps[3]=2 ('ABAB' — 'AB'), lps[4]=0 ('ABABC' — no match), lps[7]=3 ('ABABCABA' — 'ABA'). During search, when mismatch at j, reset j=lps[j-1] instead of 0 — reusing matched prefix knowledge.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **In interviews, KMP is the expected answer for 'O(n+m) string matching'.** The hardest part is building the failure function — practise explaining it as: 'lps[i] is the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that is also a suffix'. This definition makes the sliding logic self-explanatory. Rabin-Karp shines when searching for *multiple* patterns simultaneously (compute all pattern hashes, check the set on each window) or when the alphabet is large. The naive algorithm is fine for O(n·m) problems and interview warm-ups — always clarify constraints before choosing.

items: **Naive search** compares pattern at every text position — O(n·m) worst case, simple to implement, sufficient for small inputs.

**KMP** preprocesses the pattern to build the **failure function** (lps array) in O(m), encoding the longest prefix-suffix at each position. Searching uses this to skip redundant comparisons — total O(n+m) worst case.
The **failure function** `lps[j]` defines where to resume pattern matching after a mismatch at position j: resume at `lps[j-1]` rather than restarting from 0.
**Rabin-Karp** uses a **rolling hash** to compare text windows to the pattern hash in O(1) per shift — O(n+m) expected, O(n·m) worst case (hash collisions); excellent for multi-pattern search.
All three algorithms are O(n+m) or better in expected/amortised terms; KMP guarantees O(n+m) worst case without any collision risk.

quiz.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of the naive string matching algorithm on text length n and pattern length m?
options: O(n + m)
O(n log m)
O(n * m)
O(m²)
quiz.explanation: The naive algorithm tries all n−m+1 starting positions and compares up to m characters at each. The adversarial case is text='AAAA...A' and pattern='AAA...AB': m-1 characters match at every position before failing, giving O(n·m) total comparisons.

quiz.question: What does the KMP failure function (lps array) store at position j?
options: The position of the last mismatch in pattern[0..j]
The length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..j] that is also a suffix
The number of characters matched so far at position j
The index in the text where the pattern last matched
quiz.explanation: lps[j] (Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix) stores the length of the longest proper prefix of the substring pattern[0..j] that is also a suffix of that substring. 'Proper' means the prefix is not the entire string. This value tells KMP where to resume pattern matching after a mismatch.

quiz.question: For pattern 'ABAAB', what is lps[4] (0-indexed, for the full pattern)?
quiz.explanation: Pattern[0..4] = 'ABAAB'. Proper prefixes: A, AB, ABA, ABAA. Check which is also a suffix: 'AB' is a prefix (length 2) — is 'AB' a suffix of 'ABAAB'? Yes ('ABAAB' ends in 'AB'). 'ABA' (length 3) — is 'ABAAB' ending in 'ABA'? No. So the longest is 'AB', lps[4] = 2.

quiz.question: When KMP finds a mismatch at pattern position j (and j > 0), what does it do next?
options: Reset j to 0 and increment the text index i
Set j = lps[j-1] without moving the text index i backwards
Decrement text index i by j positions and reset j to 0
Skip m positions in the text to the next potential match
quiz.explanation: On mismatch at pattern[j], KMP sets j = lps[j-1] — falling back to the longest prefix of the already-matched prefix that could still extend to a match. Crucially, the text index i is never decremented. This is why KMP runs in O(n): i only moves forward, and j can decrease but the total number of decrements is bounded by the number of increments.

quiz.question: What is the total time complexity of KMP (preprocessing + searching)?
options: O(m) preprocessing + O(n*m) searching = O(n*m)
O(m) preprocessing + O(n) searching = O(n+m)
O(m log m) preprocessing + O(n log n) searching = O(n log n)
O(1) preprocessing + O(n+m) searching = O(n+m)
quiz.explanation: Building the lps array takes O(m) — each position is processed once with the two-pointer technique. Searching takes O(n) — the text pointer i never moves backwards, so it advances at most n times. Total: O(m) + O(n) = O(n+m). This is optimal since you must read all n+m characters at least once.

quiz.question: How does Rabin-Karp update the window hash when sliding one position to the right?
options: Recompute the hash of the new window from scratch — O(m) per slide
Remove the leftmost character's contribution and add the new rightmost character — O(1) per slide
XOR the old hash with the removed character and new character
Multiply the hash by a fixed constant and take mod
quiz.explanation: The rolling hash formula allows O(1) updates: new_hash = (old_hash - char_removed * BASE^(m-1)) * BASE + char_added (all mod a prime). This removes the leftmost character's contribution (scaled by its position weight) and appends the new character. This is the key insight that gives Rabin-Karp its O(n) search phase.

quiz.question: Why does Rabin-Karp do a full character-by-character comparison when hashes match?
options: To compute the next hash value more efficiently
Because hash collisions can cause false positives — two different strings may have the same hash
Character comparison is faster than arithmetic for short patterns
To update the failure function for the next search
quiz.explanation: Hash functions map many strings to the same hash value (collision). A hash match means the strings might be equal, but not certainly. The full comparison (O(m)) confirms true matches. In practice with a large prime modulus, collisions are rare, so most windows are rejected in O(1) by hash comparison alone.

quiz.question: Rabin-Karp's worst-case time complexity is O(n*m). When does this occur?
options: When the text and pattern are both very long
When the hash function produces a collision at every window position
When the pattern appears at every position in the text
When the BASE value is chosen as 1
quiz.explanation: If the hash function collides at every window (hash(window) = hash(pattern) for all n−m+1 windows), Rabin-Karp falls back to character comparison at every position — O(m) per position, O(n·m) total. This is contrived with a good hash function but theoretically possible. KMP avoids this with its guaranteed O(n+m).

quiz.question: You need to find all occurrences of any of 100 different patterns in a large text. Which algorithm is most naturally suited?
options: KMP — run 100 separate KMP searches
Naive — simplest to extend to multiple patterns
Rabin-Karp — hash all 100 patterns into a set, check each window against the set in O(1)
DFS on a suffix tree
quiz.explanation: Rabin-Karp extends naturally to multi-pattern search: precompute hashes for all 100 patterns, store in a hash set, then slide one window across the text checking if the window hash is in the set — O(1) per window. KMP would need 100 separate O(n) passes or a more complex construction. Rabin-Karp solves the multi-pattern case in O(n + total pattern length) expected.

quiz.question: Text='AAAA', Pattern='AAA'. How many matches does KMP find, and at what indices?
options: 1 match at index 0
2 matches at indices 0 and 1
3 matches at indices 0, 1, and 2
4 matches at indices 0, 1, 2, and 3
quiz.explanation: Pattern length m=3, text length n=4. Valid starting positions: 0 and 1 (0 ≤ i ≤ n−m = 1). Text[0..2]='AAA' = pattern ✓ (match at 0). Text[1..3]='AAA' = pattern ✓ (match at 1). So 2 matches at indices 0 and 1. After finding the match at index 0, KMP uses lps[m-1] = lps[2] = 2 to slide and find the next match efficiently.
